passage: Puttar, nervous about your dastar bandi next month? So was I. I was eleven, in our village near Moga. The whole gurdwara was watching while Bhai-ji tied my first turban. It felt so heavy. My friend Manoj, who came with his family, gave me a thumbs-up from the back. I was proud and wanted to run away, both at once. Afterwards I asked my Bapu-ji, 'Why do I have to wear it? What does it mean?' He could have said, 'Because.' Instead he walked me round the village pond and told me it meant I would now look after others, not just myself. That night the weight finally felt right. Your Dada-ji Gurpreet still remembers that walk.

qa.q: Who tied young Gurpreet's first turban?
qa.a: Bhai-ji.

qa.q: How did young Gurpreet feel during the ceremony?
qa.a: He felt proud and nervous at once, watched by the whole gurdwara, wanting both to stand tall and to run away.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped young Gurpreet most?
qa.a: Bapu-ji choosing to walk with him and explain what the turban meant, instead of just saying 'because', so the rite made sense.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen his friend's big day?
qa.a: Manoj seemed supportive and a little impressed, giving a thumbs-up from the back to cheer Gurpreet on.

grounding: Shows a boy at a coming-of-age rite who feels proud, nervous and watched, and whose confusion eases once an elder explains the new duty it marks.

passage: The priest was stuck in traffic, and Vaibhav's upanayana was already an hour late. Sixty guests fanned themselves in the heat. Vaibhav, nine, sat on the low stool with his head freshly shaved and the new sacred thread on a plate beside him, feeling every eye on his bare scalp. 'Why am I doing this?' he whispered to his cousin Lokesh, who had had his own two years ago. 'Nobody told me what it's for.' Lokesh crouched beside him. 'It means you start learning properly now. Prayers, and being responsible. You'll get a new chant to remember.' When the priest finally hurried in, Vaibhav sat up straighter, still nervous, but proud now too.

qa.q: How late was the ceremony?
qa.a: An hour late.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling as he sat waiting on the low stool?
qa.a: He felt nervous, watched and confused, since no one had explained what the rite was for.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that helped, and what could the adults add?
qa.a: Lokesh explained the meaning simply; the adults could also have explained it to Vaibhav before the day.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt being asked by his younger cousin?
qa.a: Lokesh probably felt trusted and a bit grown-up, remembering his own ceremony and wanting to ease Vaibhav's nerves.

grounding: Illustrates a boy at his upanayana who feels nervous, watched and confused until the meaning of the new duty is explained, and then feels proud as well.

passage:
In the village near Rampur, the whole mohalla crowded into the courtyard for Asif's Ameen, the day he finished reading the Quran through for the first time. Asif, ten, sat on a new mat in a stiff white kurta beside the maulvi sahab, forty faces watching.

His hands were sweating. What if he stumbled on the last verse?

He didn't. When he finished, everyone said "Ameen" so loudly that the pigeons flew off the roof. Nani pressed a garland over his head.

Later his schoolteacher, Alka ma'am, who had come with sweets, asked, "What does it mean for you now?"

Asif thought. "Abbu says now I should read it myself and understand it, not just say it." He frowned. "I'm not sure how to understand it yet."

"Then that's the next part," she said.

qa.q: What did everyone say together when Asif finished?
qa.a: Everyone said "Ameen" so loudly that the pigeons flew off the roof.

qa.q: How did Asif feel before the last verse?
qa.a: Asif felt nervous, hands sweating, afraid he might stumble with forty faces watching.

qa.q: What could help Asif with 'the next part'?
qa.a: Someone like Abbu or the maulvi sahab explaining the meaning with him, so the rite's new duty makes sense.

qa.q: How might Nani feel as she places the garland?
qa.a: Nani likely feels proud and joyful, marking Asif's step in front of the whole mohalla.

grounding: Shows a boy at a faith rite of passage feeling proud, nervous and watched, and unsure of its meaning until it is explained.

passage:
In the church in Beirut, Sami, eight, stood in the line of children in white, his new shoes pinching. His grandmother had pressed his shirt twice. His cousin Tariq, who had made his first communion the year before, winked from the pew.

Sami's stomach fluttered. Everyone was watching: his parents, both grandmothers, the neighbours from the third floor.

When his turn came he remembered to fold his hands, and he didn't trip. Afterwards the family took eleven photos on the steps.

At lunch he whispered to Tariq, "What was supposed to feel different?"

Tariq shrugged. "Teta says it means you're bigger now in church. You take part properly."

Sami chewed on that with his almond cake. He felt proud. He also still didn't quite know what had changed.

qa.q: How many photos did the family take on the steps?
qa.a: The family took eleven photos on the steps.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Sami have after the ceremony?
qa.a: Sami felt proud of doing it right, yet confused about what was supposed to feel different.

qa.q: What would help Sami understand the rite?
qa.a: An adult, perhaps Teta or the priest, sitting with him to explain what the step means and what he now takes part in.

qa.q: How might Tariq see Sami's question?
qa.a: Tariq takes it lightly, sharing Teta's simple explanation, maybe because he wondered the same last year.

grounding: Shows a child at a coming-of-age rite in another faith feeling proud, nervous and watched, and confused about its meaning.

passage:
In the catechism hall behind the church in Kottayam, twelve children waited on benches for their first confession. Thomas, nine, kept rehearsing: "I fought with my sister. I lied about homework." His palms were damp.

"Why do we have to tell the priest?" he whispered to Rashmi teacher. "God already knows."

She knelt by the bench. "It's a way of saying it out loud, so you can let it go. After this you're ready for your first communion. It's a new step: you take part more fully."

"What if I forget something?"

"Then you say what you remember. That's enough."

When he came out of the little room, his shoulders had dropped. He sat down and turned to the boy beside him. "It's okay," he said. "It's quick."

qa.q: How many children waited for their first confession?
qa.a: Twelve children waited on benches.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel while waiting?
qa.a: Thomas felt nervous, rehearsing with damp palms, and confused about why he had to say it aloud.

qa.q: What did Rashmi teacher do that helped?
qa.a: She knelt and explained the meaning simply, and reassured him that saying what he remembers is enough.

qa.q: What might the boy beside Thomas feel when told 'It's quick'?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and less anxious, hearing it from someone who has just done it.

grounding: Shows a child at a rite of passage in his faith feeling nervous and confused until an adult explains what the new step means.

passage:
Two weeks before: Thomas, eleven, practised in the Kottayam church every Saturday, walking slowly with folded hands. His friend Chinmay asked, "What's First Communion?" Thomas shrugged. "Something big. Everyone's coming." His stomach twisted.
The day: In his new white suit, Thomas walked up the aisle feeling every eye on him. His grandmother was crying. He was proud and terrified at once. His hands shook as he received the bread. He did everything right, but he didn't know what it meant.
The next week: Chinmay asked again. Thomas asked Ammachi, who explained it was a way of joining the church family, and that he would now go to Mass like the grown-ups. "It's a new duty, and a gift." Thomas repeated it to Chinmay. It made more sense when he said it himself.

qa.q: What did Thomas wear on the day?
qa.a: His new white suit.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel walking up the aisle?
qa.a: He felt proud and terrified at once, his hands shaking with everyone watching.

qa.q: What helped Thomas understand the rite?
qa.a: Ammachi explaining its meaning afterwards, and then Thomas explaining it to Chinmay in his own words.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see the rite, coming from outside it?
qa.a: Chinmay was curious and puzzled at first, and probably found it clearer once Thomas explained it simply.

grounding: It illustrates a child at a coming-of-age rite in another faith who feels proud, nervous and watched, and confused until the meaning is explained.
